claim: Cells adapt to familiar changes in their environment by activating predefined regulatory programs that establish adaptive gene expression states.
source: Cells adapt to familiar changes in their environment by activating predefined regulatory programs that establish adaptive gene expression states.
evidence: This is a general statement about cellular adaptation supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Hard-wired pathways may be inadequate for adaptation to environments never encountered before.
source: These hard-wired pathways, however, may be inadequate for adaptation to environments never encountered before.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the limitations of hard-wired pathways.

claim: Individual genes can achieve optimal expression levels through a stochastic search for improved fitness.
source: Instead, individual genes achieve optimal expression levels through a stochastic search for improved fitness.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the manuscript, supported by experimental data and simulations presented throughout.

claim: Stochastic tuning enables adaptation to adverse conditions without relying on external sensory information or genetically predetermined cis-regulation.
source: Here, we reveal evidence for an alternative mode of gene regulation that enables adaptation to adverse conditions without relying on external sensory information or genetically predetermined cis-regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental evidence showing URA3 expression tuning in synthetic promoters lacking transcription factor binding sites.

claim: Stochastic tuning discovers global gene expression states that are fundamentally new and yet optimized for novel environments.
source: By focusing on improving the overall health of the cell, the proposed stochastic tuning mechanism discovers global gene expression states that are fundamentally new and yet optimized for novel environments.
evidence: This is supported by simulations and experimental data showing adaptation to novel environments.

claim: Stochastic tuning operates in Saccharomyces cerevisiae adapting to laboratory-engineered environments foreign to its native gene-regulatory network.
source: We provide experimental evidence for stochastic tuning in the adaptation of Saccharomyces cerevisiae to laboratory-engineered environments that are foreign to its native gene-regulatory network.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data showing colony formation and URA3 expression changes.

claim: Stochastic tuning operates locally at individual gene promoters.
source: Stochastic tuning operates locally at individual gene promoters, and its efficacy is modulated by perturbations to chromatin modification machinery.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data showing allele-specific changes in URA3 expression.

claim: The efficacy of stochastic tuning is modulated by perturbations to chromatin modification machinery.
source: Stochastic tuning operates locally at individual gene promoters, and its efficacy is modulated by perturbations to chromatin modification machinery.
evidence: This is supported by data showing effects of GCN5 and ASF1 deletions on tuning rates.

claim: Dedicated sensory, signaling, and regulatory networks become inadequate or detrimental when cells are exposed to unfamiliar environments foreign to their evolutionary history.
source: However, dedicated sensory, signaling, and regulatory networks become inadequate, or even detrimental, when cells are exposed to unfamiliar environments that are foreign to their evolutionary history (Tagkopoulos et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Under any conceivable environment, at least one gene expression state that maximizes the health/fitness of the cell always exists.
source: In principle, at least one gene expression state that maximizes the health/fitness of the cell always exists, despite the inability of the native regulatory network to establish such a state.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement based on logical reasoning.

claim: Under any environment, the activities of some genes are beneficial, whereas those of others are futile or even actively detrimental.
source: This is true because under any conceivable environment, the activities of some genes are beneficial, whereas those of others are futile or even actively detrimental (Jacob and Monod, 1961; Tagkopoulos et al., 2008; Hottes et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A population of cells may slowly adapt to an unfamiliar environment through the accumulation of genetic mutations that rewire regulatory networks.
source: In fact, if the initial fitness defect is not lethal, a population of cells may slowly adapt to an unfamiliar environment through the accumulation of genetic mutations that rewire regulatory networks, thereby achieving more optimal gene expression states (Tagkopoulos et al., 2008; Applebee et al., 2008; Philippe et al., 2007; Goodarzi et al., 2010; Tenaillon et al., 2012; Rodríguez-Verdugo et al., 2016; Blount et al., 2012; Van Hofwegen et al., 2016; Damkiær et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Stochastic tuning requires a source of stochastic transitions in gene expression.
source: We reasoned that such an optimization process would require the existence of: (1) a source of stochastic transitions in gene expression
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement for the proposed mechanism.

claim: Stochastic tuning requires the ability of local chromatin to maintain a record of recent changes in transcription.
source: We reasoned that such an optimization process would require the existence of: (1) a source of stochastic transitions in gene expression; (2) the ability of local chromatin to maintain a record of recent changes in transcription
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement for the proposed mechanism.

claim: Stochastic tuning requires a central metabolic hub that integrates diverse parameters of intracellular health and continuously broadcasts whether the overall health of the cell is improving or deteriorating.
source: We reasoned that such an optimization process would require the existence of: (1) a source of stochastic transitions in gene expression; (2) the ability of local chromatin to maintain a record of recent changes in transcription; and (3) a central metabolic hub that integrates diverse parameters of intracellular health and continuously broadcasts whether the overall health of the cell is improving or deteriorating.
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement for the proposed mechanism.

claim: The expression of many genes is dominated by noisy bursts of transcription.
source: The expression of many genes is dominated by noisy bursts of transcription—a widespread phenomenon of largely unknown functional significance (Sanchez and Golding, 2013; Raj and van Oudenaarden, 2008; Blake et al., 2006; Raser and O'Shea, 2005; Elowitz et al., 2002)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Co-transcriptional histone modification can modify eukaryotic chromatin in promoters and gene bodies, establishing a short-term memory of recent transcriptional events.
source: Co-transcriptional histone modification can modify eukaryotic chromatin in promoters and gene bodies, establishing a short-term memory of recent transcriptional events (Li et al., 2007; Rando and Winston, 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Global integrators of cell health have evolved in eukaryotes.
source: Global integrators of cell health have evolved in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a general statement about eukaryotic cell biology.

claim: The mTOR pathway integrates a vast array of intracellular parameters reflecting nutrient availability, energy, and the presence of diverse stresses.
source: A classic example is the mTOR pathway, which integrates a vast array of intracellular parameters reflecting nutrient availability, energy, and the presence of diverse stresses (Conrad et al., 2014; González and Hall, 2017; Albert and Hall, 2015; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: If global fitness/health is increasing and there was a previous increase in transcriptional output, the promoter further increases its transcriptional activity.
source: if global fitness/health is increasing and there was a previous increase in transcriptional output (representing larger or more frequent transcriptional bursts), the promoter further increases its transcriptional activity (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the logic of the proposed stochastic tuning mechanism, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: If fitness is decreasing and there was a previous increase in transcriptional activity, the promoter decreases its transcriptional output.
source: If fitness is decreasing and there was a previous increase in transcriptional activity, the promoter decreases its transcriptional output.
evidence: This describes the logic of the proposed stochastic tuning mechanism.

claim: The stochastic tuning mechanism can find near-optimal gene-expression states for a system with thousands of genes.
source: What is remarkable, however, is the ability of this hypothetical stochastic tuning process to find near-optimal gene-expression states for a system with thousands of genes.
evidence: This is supported by simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Stochastic tuning is achieved through a fitness-directed stochastic search culminating in individual genes reaching specific gene expression levels that maximize the health/fitness of the cell.
source: As can be seen in the simulations presented in Figure 2, this is achieved through a fitness-directed stochastic search culminating in individual genes reaching specific gene expression levels that maximize the health/fitness of the cell.
evidence: This is supported by simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Stochastic tuning would enable free-living organisms to optimize their global gene expression patterns to match the specific requirements of any environment in which their dedicated sensory and regulatory networks are inadequate or sub-optimal.
source: Such a stochastic tuning mechanism would be highly valuable to free-living organisms, enabling them to optimize their global gene expression patterns to match the specific requirements of any environment in which their dedicated sensory and regulatory networks are inadequate or sub-optimal.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential value of stochastic tuning.

claim: A yeast strain (BY4743) lacks the URA3 gene, which is essential when cells are grown in the absence of uracil.
source: This was achieved by using a yeast strain (BY4743) that lacks the URA3 gene, which is essential when cells are grown in the absence of uracil.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: A chromosomally integrated copy of URA3 was placed at a different locus under the control of a weak synthetic promoter consisting primarily of a pseudorandom sequence.
source: We placed a chromosomally integrated copy of URA3 at a different locus under the control of a weak synthetic promoter, consisting primarily of a pseudorandom sequence.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: All recognizable binding sites for native transcription factors were removed from the generated promoter sequence.
source: All recognizable binding sites for native transcription factors were removed from the generated promoter sequence (see Materials and Methods and Supplementary file 1 for details)
evidence: This describes the experimental design to decouple the promoter from existing regulatory input.

claim: 6-azauracil (6AU) was added to the media to control the threshold level of URA3 production required for growth.
source: We also added the URA3 competitive antagonist 6-azauracil (6AU) to the media to control the threshold level of URA3 production required for growth.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: Cells containing synprom-driven URA3 show apparently stochastic transitions to rapid growth after prolonged incubation on ura-/6AU15 plates.
source: Remarkably, however, after prolonged incubation we observed apparently stochastic transitions to rapid growth, leading to the formation of macroscopic colonies over time (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Colony formation occurs at a rate of roughly one cell in 10^3, which is too high to be driven by mutation-driven adaptation in the absence of growth.
source: We eventually observed colony formation by roughly one cell in 103, a rate too high to be driven by mutation-driven adaptation in the absence of growth.
evidence: This is based on observed colony formation rates and reasoning about mutation rates.

claim: Four of the six synthetic promoters support stochastic tuning.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, four of the six synthetic promoters support stochastic tuning
evidence: This is shown in the supplementary figure data.

claim: The ability of synprom5 to undergo tuning remains even with a different promoter proximal region.
source: and the ability of synprom5 (the purely artificial component of the synprom referred to in the remainder of the text; see Supplementary file 2 for all synthetic promoter sequences) to undergo tuning remains even with a different promoter proximal region.
evidence: This is shown in the supplementary figure data.

claim: Similar tuning behavior was observed for two high-noise natural promoters, PHSP12 and PRGI1.
source: As shown in Figure 3C, we also observed similar tuning behavior for two high-noise natural promoters, PHSP12 and PRGI1 (Tirosh et al., 2009; Tirosh et al., 2006)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Stochastic tuning can function even when superimposed on naturally evolved regulatory sites.
source: indicating that stochastic tuning can function even when superimposed on naturally evolved regulatory sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that natural promoters also show tuning behavior.

claim: Tuning rates varied from 1 in 10^1 (PHSP12) to 1 in 10^5 (synprom5-arf1).
source: Across all promoters (natural and synthetic) tested here, the observed tuning rates, relative to the number of viable plated cells, varied from 1 in 101 (PHSP12) to 1 in 105 (synprom5-arf1).
evidence: This is based on observed colony formation rates.

claim: The apparently stochastic nature of colony formation is reflected in the steady emergence of colonies over the course of days or weeks.
source: The apparently stochastic nature of colony formation in our experiments is reflected both in the steady emergence of colonies over the course of days or weeks (Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: The apparently stochastic nature of colony formation is reflected in the wide variance of colony sizes observed on ura-/6AU15 plates.
source: and in the wide variance of colony sizes observed on ura-/6AU15 plates (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cells remain quiescent for days before transitioning to URA3 expression and rapid growth.
source: Microscopy revealed that cells remain quiescent for days before transitioning to URA3 expression and rapid growth, with a transition rate dependent on the choice of promoter (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is observed in microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The change that enables growth under the ura-/6AU15 condition must be passed from mother to daughter cells.
source: Furthermore, the change that enables growth under the ura-/6AU15 condition must be passed from mother to daughter cells, as colonies expand from a few points of initiation instead of showing random division of cells throughout the microscopic field over time.
evidence: This is inferred from microscopy observations.

claim: The appearance of colonies is not simply due to aging of the plates.
source: We confirmed that the appearance of colonies is not simply due to aging of the plates; 6AU-containing plates which were pre-incubated for a week or longer prior to plating of cells showed no change in colony formation rates (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on control experiments.

claim: URA3-mRuby fluorescence increases substantially in tandem with the onset of cell growth in synprom-URA3-mRuby/PADH1-DHFR-GFP cells.
source: In the case of URA3-mRuby driven by synprom and DHFR-GFP by the constitutive promoter PADH1, URA3-mRuby fluorescence increases substantially in tandem with the onset of cell growth, and expression subsequently remains high until saturation
evidence: This is observed in flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: DHFR-GFP signals do not recover to their initial levels in synprom-URA3-mRuby/PADH1-DHFR-GFP cells during tuning.
source: in contrast, DHFR-GFP signals do not even recover to their initial levels (Figure 4B; compare dashed and solid line distributions).
evidence: This is observed in flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The URA3 induction resulting in growth is promoter-specific and does not simply reflect a general increase in protein expression.
source: This demonstrates that the URA3 induction resulting in growth is promoter-specific and does not simply reflect a general increase in protein expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential behavior of URA3-mRuby and DHFR-GFP.

claim: For cells with synprom driving both fluorescent fusions, there is a specific enhancement of URA3-mRuby expression over that of DHFR-GFP.
source: Even more strikingly, for cells with synprom driving both fluorescent fusions, we observed a specific enhancement of URA3-mRuby expression over that of DHFR-GFP (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is observed in flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The transition to high URA3 expression is allele-specific and must be driven at least partly by changes occurring in cis at the specific locus whose expression is required for growth.
source: showing that the transition to high URA3 expression is not only promoter-specific but allele-specific, and thus must be driven at least partly by changes occurring in cis at the specific locus whose expression is required for growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential expression of URA3 and DHFR driven by the same promoter.

claim: There is a substantial increase in the URA3:DHFR ratio in tuned cells in liquid ura-/6AU5 media.
source: In both cases, we observed a substantial increase in the URA3:DHFR ratio in the tuned cells, indicating that the observed tuning occurs at least partly through a local cis-acting process at the locus required for growth
evidence: This is shown in RT-qPCR data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a substantial increase in the URA3:DHFR ratio in tuned cells on ura-/6AU15 plates.
source: In both cases, we observed a substantial increase in the URA3:DHFR ratio in the tuned cells, indicating that the observed tuning occurs at least partly through a local cis-acting process at the locus required for growth
evidence: This is shown in RT-qPCR data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The allele-specific nature of the transcriptional induction supports a key role for a local tuning process that is independent of dedicated sensory and regulatory input.
source: Consistent with our proposed tuning model, the allele-specific nature of the transcriptional induction supports a key role for a local tuning process that is independent of dedicated sensory and regulatory input.
evidence: This is inferred from the allele-specific expression changes.

claim: In the low 6AU case, the tuning mechanism pushes URA3 expression almost deterministically to its optimal (high) value.
source: In the low 6AU case, the tuning mechanism pushes URA3 expression almost deterministically to its optimal (high) value
evidence: This is shown in simulations in Figure 5A.

claim: In the presence of high 6AU, the URA3 expression level undergoes a random walk until expression becomes high enough to allow the tuning mechanism to 'sense' the gradient and drive the cells into a URA3+ state.
source: whereas in the presence of high 6AU, the URA3 expression level undergoes a random walk until expression becomes high enough to allow the tuning mechanism to 'sense' the gradient and drive the cells into a URA3+ state.
evidence: This is shown in simulations in Figure 5A.

claim: Increasing 6AU concentrations both slow tuning and dramatically increase the variance in the amount of time required for each individual cell to reach a URA+ state.
source: The effects on tuning rates of varying the 6AU concentration are plotted in Figure 5B, where we observe that increasing 6AU concentrations both slow tuning and dramatically increase the variance in the amount of time required for each individual cell to reach a URA+ state.
evidence: This is shown in simulations in Figure 5B.

claim: Tuning in the experimental system switched from slow and stochastic to rapid and deterministic in the presence of low 6AU concentrations.
source: On the other hand, tuning in our experimental system switched from slow and stochastic to rapid and deterministic in the presence of low 6AU concentrations, with observable tuning occurring over the course of a few hours (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in experimental data in Figure 5C.

claim: The tuning process is confined to the URA3-mRuby allele in low 6AU conditions, despite DHFR-GFP being driven by the same synthetic promoter.
source: Importantly, the tuning process is confined to the URA3-mRuby allele, despite the fact that DHFR-GFP is also being driven by the same synthetic promoter.
evidence: This is shown in experimental data in Figure 5C.

claim: Gene expression fluctuations that surpassed a threshold for alleviating the URA3 deficit were reinforced over long timescales and were sustained (inherited) across multiple generations as the tuned colony expanded.
source: Consistent with our proposed tuning model, gene expression fluctuations that surpassed a threshold for alleviating the URA3 deficit were reinforced over long timescales and were sustained (inherited) across multiple generations as the tuned colony expanded (Figure 6).
evidence: This is observed in time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 6.

claim: There is no accompanying increase in DHFR-GFP during URA3-mRuby tuning.
source: As expected, there is no accompanying increase in DHFR-GFP.
evidence: This is observed in microscopy data.

claim: For cells growing under uracil-replete conditions (SC+glu), the mixing time is on the order of ~100 min.
source: For cells growing under uracil-replete conditions (SC+glu), we observed a relatively fast mixing time on the order of ~100 min (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is measured in FACS-based mixing time experiments.

claim: Cells starving in ura-/6AU10 media had mixing times that ranged from 400 to 1200 min.
source: On the other hand, cells starving in ura-/6AU10 media had mixing times that ranged from 400 to 1200 min (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is measured in FACS-based mixing time experiments.

claim: Dividing cells have significantly higher levels of mRuby than non-dividing cells.
source: By comparing the fluorescence of cells that are about to divide with those that are not, we found that dividing cells have significantly higher levels of mRuby than non-dividing cells, whereas the separation was much smaller for GFP (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is shown in microscopy data in Figure 7C.

claim: The URA3-mRuby levels within the tuning colony are highly heritable.
source: Furthermore, the URA3-mRuby levels within the tuning colony were highly heritable; as seen in Figure 7D, as the indicated colony tunes and grows, cells within that colony maintain a high-mRuby state through subsequent divisions, and even their internal rankings are mostly preserved.
evidence: This is shown in lineage tracking data in Figure 7D.

claim: The ratio of mRuby to GFP levels became steadily higher in cell lineages that had been dividing for longer.
source: Consistent with our expectation, we observed that the ratio of mRuby to GFP levels (the latter of which is fused to a gene whose product is not needed for growth) became steadily higher in cell lineages that had been dividing for longer (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is shown in microscopy data in Figure 7E.

claim: The level of URA3 expression is correlated with fitness.
source: These observations demonstrate that the level of URA3 expression is correlated with fitness, is transmitted across several generations, and shows an ongoing upward trend in tuned cells over the course of time.
evidence: This is inferred from microscopy observations showing higher URA3 in dividing cells.

claim: URA3 expression is transmitted across several generations.
source: These observations demonstrate that the level of URA3 expression is correlated with fitness, is transmitted across several generations, and shows an ongoing upward trend in tuned cells over the course of time.
evidence: This is shown in lineage tracking data.

claim: URA3 expression shows an ongoing upward trend in tuned cells over the course of time.
source: These observations demonstrate that the level of URA3 expression is correlated with fitness, is transmitted across several generations, and shows an ongoing upward trend in tuned cells over the course of time.
evidence: This is shown in microscopy data in Figure 7E.

claim: A directed increase in URA3 once a lineage begins growing is predicted by the model for fitness-directed tuning.
source: That last finding is particularly important because a directed increase in URA3 once a lineage begins growing is predicted by our model for fitness-directed tuning, but cannot be explained by other competing hypotheses.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model.

claim: The ongoing emergence of the tuned state in non-growing cells over the course of many days makes mutational mechanisms unlikely.
source: The ongoing emergence of the tuned state in non-growing cells, over the course of many days, makes mutational mechanisms unlikely.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed kinetics of colony formation.

claim: No more than 1–3 cell divisions occur prior to the onset of sustained growth in a small fraction of cells.
source: In addition, as seen by microscopy (Figure 3E), no more than 1–3 cell divisions occur prior to the onset of sustained growth in a small fraction of cells.
evidence: This is observed in microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Cells with synprom-driven URA3 show reversion toward the naïve colony formation rates upon growth in (uracil containing) SC+glu media.
source: As seen in Figure 8A, cells with synprom-driven URA3 show reversion toward the naïve colony formation rates upon growth in (uracil containing) SC+glu media, with recovery apparent even after a single round of growth on an SC+glu plate, and subsequently becoming stronger with additional SC+glu passages.
evidence: This is shown in experimental data in Figure 8A.

claim: Of eight isolates sequenced, five show no mutations within 25 kb of the URA3-mRuby insertion.
source: The results are summarized in Supplementary file 4: Of the eight isolates, five show no mutations within 25 kb of the URA3-mRuby insertion
evidence: This is from whole genome sequencing data.

claim: Two isolates show SNPs of unknown fitness contribution in a minority of the population.
source: two show SNPs of unknown fitness contribution in a minority of the population
evidence: This is from whole genome sequencing data.

claim: One isolate shows a duplication of the URA3-mRuby cassette.
source: and one shows a duplication of the URA3-mRuby cassette (based on the presence of a read density that is twice the level observed elsewhere for the same chromosome).
evidence: This is from whole genome sequencing data.

claim: The origin of growth-supporting URA3 expression levels in these cells cannot be reliant on a mutational mechanism.
source: These data clearly indicate that the origin of growth-supporting URA3 expression levels in these cells cannot be reliant on a mutational mechanism, as only one of the eight cases – that with the URA3 duplication -- shows a mutation at high enough levels in the population to explain the onset of growth
evidence: This is inferred from the sequencing data showing most isolates lack mutations.

claim: Highly fluorescent cells do not form colonies on ura-/6AU plates at rates substantially higher than unsorted cells.
source: These experiments clearly showed that the ability to form colonies on ura-/6AU plates is not restricted to cells with initially high URA3-mRuby expression (Supplementary file 5), as the highly fluorescent cells do not form colonies on ura-/6AU plates at rates substantially higher than unsorted cells
evidence: This is from FACS sorting experiments.

claim: Growth does not occur only in cells that already have high levels of URA3 expression at the time of plating.
source: These data argue against the possibility that growth occurs only in cells that, by chance, already have high levels of URA3 expression at the time of plating
evidence: This is inferred from FACS sorting experiments.

claim: Deletion of GCN5 essentially abolished tuning.
source: we found that genetic perturbations to the histone acetylation machinery through deletion of the key histone acetyltransferase GCN5 essentially abolished tuning
evidence: This is shown in experimental data in Figure 8B.

claim: Deletion of ASF1 increased tuning rate by more than an order of magnitude.
source: whereas deletion of the histone chaperone ASF1, in contrast, increased tuning rate by more than an order of magnitude (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is shown in experimental data in Figure 8B.

claim: The observed tuning process does not rely on transcriptional memory mechanisms grounded in chromatin localization.
source: At the same time, we show that the observed tuning process does not rely on transcriptional memory mechanisms grounded in chromatin localization, given the lack of effect of a NUP42 deletion (Figure 8B; cf. (Guan et al., 2012)).
evidence: This is shown in experimental data in Figure 8B.

claim: The effects of a mutation on survival and tuning rates are not significantly correlated.
source: As shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2, the effects of a mutation on survival and tuning rates are not significantly correlated.
evidence: This is shown in experimental data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Chemical inhibition of sirtuin HDACs by nicotinamide treatment substantially accelerated the decay of a tuned population to the naïve state.
source: As shown in Figure 8A, we found that chemical inhibition of sirtuin HDACs by nicotinamide treatment substantially accelerated the decay of a tuned population to the naïve state
evidence: This is shown in experimental data in Figure 8A.

claim: Chromatin modifications play a central role in the establishment and maintenance of the tuning process.
source: Combined with the data on knockout strains described above, our results suggest a central role for chromatin modifications in the establishment and maintenance of the tuning process
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of genetic and chemical perturbations to chromatin machinery.

claim: The detailed model is capable of stochastic tuning of a single gene which strongly impacts the fitness of the cell.
source: As shown in Figure 9C, the detailed model is capable of stochastic tuning of a single gene which strongly impacts the fitness of the cell (as would be the case for URA3 in our experimental setup).
evidence: This is shown in simulation data in Figure 9C.

claim: For most randomly generated gene-level parameters, stochastic tuning results in substantially higher fitness compared to when cells undergo random fluctuations in transcription levels or when transcription is fixed at a rate appropriate for a different environment.
source: For most randomly generated gene-level parameters, stochastic tuning results in substantially higher fitness compared to when cells undergo random fluctuations in transcription levels or when transcription is fixed at a rate appropriate for a different environment
evidence: This is shown in simulation data in Figure 9C.

claim: The model is robust to variations in both the sampled biological parameters and the parameters of the model itself.
source: The model is robust to variations in both the sampled biological parameters (Figure 9C) and the parameters of the model itself (Figure 9D)
evidence: This is shown in simulation data in Figures 9C and 9D.

claim: The model can locate an optimal expression level regardless of the ratio between the initial and target protein levels.
source: and can locate an optimal expression level regardless of the ratio between the initial and target protein levels (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is shown in simulation data in Figure 9E.

claim: Hard-coded sensory and regulatory networks are unlikely to have the encoding capacity to optimally respond to every conceivable subtle change in the environment.
source: Indeed, hard-coded sensory and regulatory networks are unlikely to have the encoding capacity to optimally respond to every conceivable subtle change in the environment—even within the native habitat.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the limitations of hard-wired networks.

claim: Dedicated regulatory networks quickly move the system to a state reasonably well matched to a given condition, and stochastic tuning subsequently optimizes expression to achieve a more precisely adapted state for every individual encounter.
source: We therefore favor a model in which dedicated regulatory networks quickly move the system to a state reasonably well matched to a given condition, and stochastic tuning subsequently optimizes expression to achieve a more precisely adapted state for every individual encounter.
evidence: This is a speculative model for how stochastic tuning and conventional regulation work together.

claim: The proposed stochastic tuning mechanism is reminiscent of the biased random walk phenomenon in bacterial chemotaxis.
source: Indeed, the proposed stochastic tuning mechanism is reminiscent of the biased random walk phenomenon in bacterial chemotaxis, where stochastic transitions in the rotation of the flagellar motor are biased towards the direction that increases chemoattractant signaling over time (Macnab and Koshland, 1972).
evidence: This is an analogy to a known biological phenomenon.

claim: Histone acetylation/deacetylation (via GCN5 and sirtuins) play a critical role in stochastic tuning.
source: In particular, histone acetylation/deacetylation (via GCN5 and sirtuins) seem to play a critical role, as deletion of GCN5 almost entirely abolished tuning.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing effects of GCN5 deletion and nicotinamide treatment.

claim: Genes regulated by the SAGA complex exhibit a high degree of intrinsic noise.
source: This is consistent with the high degree of intrinsic noise exhibited by the genes that are regulated by the SAGA complex, in which GCN5 is the catalytic subunit (Newman et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Increased transcriptional noise is beneficial for adaptation to acute environmental stress.
source: Previous work has shown that increased transcriptional noise is beneficial for adaptation to acute environmental stress (Blake et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Deletion of GCN5 increases expression noise in the context of the PHO5 promoter.
source: Interestingly, however, early work demonstrated that deletion of GCN5 further increases expression noise in the context of the PHO5 promoter (Raser and O'Shea, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Stochastic tuning is not driven by noise alone.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that stochastic tuning is not driven by noise alone
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GCN5 deletion increases noise but abolishes tuning.

claim: The proper integration of noise, transcriptional memory, chromatin modification, and cellular-health feedback work together to implement a directed search mechanism to drive the expression level of individual genes to levels that maximize the overall health of the cell.
source: rather we support a model in which the proper integration of noise, transcriptional memory, chromatin modification, and cellular-health feedback work together to implement a directed search mechanism to drive the expression level of individual genes to levels that maximize the overall health of the cell.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanistic model for stochastic tuning.

claim: Histone modification is tightly coupled with gene expression.
source: Indeed, histone modification is tightly coupled with gene expression.
evidence: This is a general statement about chromatin biology.

claim: Co-transcriptional histone modification can store recent memory of transcriptional activity.
source: Co-transcriptional histone modification can store recent memory of transcriptional activity (Li et al., 2007; Rando and Winston, 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Histone modification can affect transcription rate.
source: and histone modification can, in turn, affect transcription rate (Stasevich et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The experimental setup has superficial similarities to experiments performed by the Braun lab on GAL1 promoter repression.
source: We note that our experimental setup for demonstrating stochastic tuning has superficial similarities to a series of experiments performed in S. cerevisiae by the Braun lab, in which they sought to determine whether glucose-driven repression of the GAL1 promoter could be overcome to allow expression of a HIS3 construct in glucose-containing media (Stern et al., 2007; Stolovicki et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work.

claim: In the Braun lab experiments, genetic mutations are the primary mechanism of adaptation.
source: While the authors observed consistent emergence of growth in a large fraction of cells that they initially noted could be attributed to either genetic or epigenetic mechanisms (Stolovicki et al., 2006), subsequent analysis has shown that in that experimental system, genetic mutations are the primary mechanism of adaptation, possibly driven by hypermutability of the genes involved in the response of interest (David et al., 2010; Moore et al., 2014; David et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The mutational mechanisms in the Braun lab experiments stand in clear contrast to the rapidly reverting epigenetic stochastic tuning observed in the current experiments.
source: These mutational mechanisms stand in clear contrast to the rapidly reverting epigenetic stochastic tuning observed in our experiments.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current work and previous work.

claim: Cells possess hard-wired homeostatic mechanisms sensing and responding to internal parameters.
source: In addition to perception of environmental parameters, cells also possess a variety of hard-wired homeostatic mechanisms sensing and responding to internal parameters, optimizing resource allocation in response to parameters such as growth rate (Klumpp et al., 2009; Klumpp and Hwa, 2014; Brauer et al., 2008; Barenholz et al., 2016; Keren et al., 2013) and metabolite/nutrient pools (Potrykus et al., 2011; Broach, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hard-wired homeostatic mechanisms reflect specific evolved responses to alter resource allocation and gene expression in a predefined way in response to stress.
source: However, while these mechanisms allow cells to sense their internal state, they still reflect specific evolved responses to alter resource allocation and gene expression in a predefined way in response to stress, standing in contrast with the ability of stochastic tuning to conduct a search and discover arbitrary gene expression states that are adaptive under extreme and unfamiliar environments.
evidence: This is a comparison between conventional homeostatic mechanisms and stochastic tuning.

claim: Sequence features can influence tuning efficacy.
source: The widely varying tuning rates for different promoters (Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) clearly indicate that sequence features can influence tuning efficacy.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed variation in tuning rates across different promoters.

claim: All but one promoter driving URA3 in the experiments contained a TATA box.
source: By design, all but one promoter driving URA3 in our experiments contained a TATA box, which has been linked to high intrinsic noise (Newman et al., 2006), condition-specific expression variability (Tirosh et al., 2006) and reliance on chromatin-mediated regulation (Tirosh et al., 2008; Basehoar et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by citations.

claim: Replacement of the TATA-containing PSAM3 derived sequence in synprom with a TATA-free PARF1 sequence substantially reduced tuning rates.
source: Indeed, replacement of the (TATA-containing) PSAM3 derived sequence in synprom with a similarly generated sequence from the TATA-free PARF1 promoter substantially reduced tuning rates under the conditions tested (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PGAL1 showed dramatically lower rates of colony formation (less than 1 in 10^7), and those colonies that did form appeared to be non-reverting genetic mutants.
source: We also note that when we performed experiments similar to those described above with the repressed natural promoter PGAL1, we observed dramatically lower rates of colony formation (less than 1 in 107), and those colonies that did form appeared to be non-reverting genetic mutants (data not shown).
evidence: This is from experimental observations.

claim: Fitness-directed stochastic tuning requires feedback of the global state of health to every promoter in the genome.
source: Fitness-directed stochastic tuning requires feedback of the global state of health to every promoter in the genome.
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The dependence of many histone modification enzymes on metabolic intermediates and cofactors provides support for potential direct feedback of global fitness-related parameters to the epigenome.
source: The dependence of many histone modification enzymes on metabolic intermediates and cofactors (e.g., NAD+ for the sirtuin family of histone deacetylases (Lin et al., 2000; Thaminy et al., 2007); SAM for histone methyltransferases (Luka et al., 2009), and acetyl-CoA for histone acetyltransferases (Tanner et al., 1999)) provides support for potential direct feedback of global fitness-related parameters to the epigenome (Katada et al., 2012; Kurdistani, 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Chemical manipulation of sirtuin activity had substantial effects on retention of epigenetic memory.
source: and indeed we showed that chemical manipulation of sirtuin activity had substantial effects on retention of epigenetic memory.
evidence: This is shown in experimental data in Figure 8A.

claim: Histone modification enzymes may serve as distinct channels of health-related information utilized by stochastic tuning.
source: These enzymes may very well serve as distinct channels of health-related information utilized by stochastic tuning.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism.

claim: Chromatin itself may function as a global health integrator, with histone modifications and their effect on gene expression being highly contingent on the current trajectory of cellular fitness.
source: In this regard, chromatin itself may function as a global health integrator, with histone modifications and their effect on gene expression being highly contingent on the current trajectory of cellular fitness.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism.

claim: The mTOR pathway has been shown to regulate histone acetylation states through a variety of mechanisms.
source: Intriguingly, the mTOR pathway has recently been shown to regulate histone acetylation states through a variety of mechanisms (Chen et al., 2012; Workman et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Stochastic tuning may have initially evolved as a mechanism for adaptation of single-cell eukaryotes to extreme environments.
source: Stochastic tuning may have initially evolved as a mechanism for adaptation of single-cell eukaryotes to extreme environments.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the evolutionary origin of stochastic tuning.

claim: Stochastic tuning may have found additional utility as a versatile mechanism for controlling and fine-tuning gene expression in the context of physiological and developmental processes in metazoans.
source: However, once available, it may have found additional utility as a versatile mechanism for controlling and fine-tuning gene expression in the context of physiological and developmental processes in metazoans.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential broader role of stochastic tuning.

claim: Stochastic tuning is consistent with the evolutionary arc of an ancient set of molecular mechanisms that now serve as key mediators of differentiation.
source: This is consistent with the evolutionary arc of an ancient set of molecular mechanisms that now serve as key mediators of differentiation (Álvarez-Errico et al., 2015; Ziller et al., 2015; Meissner, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Stochastic tuning may play an important role in allowing cancer cells to survive and thrive in a variety of microenvironments unfamiliar to their evolved regulatory networks.
source: Optimization of cellular health through the fitness-directed stochastic tuning mechanism may also play an important role in allowing cancer cells to survive and thrive in a variety of microenvironments unfamiliar to their evolved regulatory networks, and in the face of extreme challenges imposed by chemotherapy and radiation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential role of stochastic tuning in cancer.

claim: Stochastic tuning may underlie the epigenetically mediated metastatic potential and chemotherapy resistance observed in a variety of cancer types.
source: Indeed, stochastic tuning may underlie the epigenetically mediated metastatic potential and chemotherapy resistance observed in a variety of cancer types (Wu and Roberts, 2013; Perez-Plasencia and Duenas-Gonzalez, 2006; Lv et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015; Borley and Brown, 2015; Bonito et al., 2016; Shaffer et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work and is speculative about the mechanism.

claim: A fitness-directed tuning process operates at the level of transcription.
source: Our observations support the existence of a fitness-directed tuning process that operates at the level of transcription.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing transcriptional changes.

claim: In principle, tuning could also occur at any point along the hierarchy of gene expression where noise, memory, and feedback of global fitness can drive the activity of gene products towards levels that optimize the overall health of the cell.
source: However, in principle, tuning could also occur at any point along the hierarchy of gene expression where noise, memory, and feedback of global fitness can drive the activity of gene products towards levels that optimize the overall health of the cell.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential broader applications of the tuning mechanism.
